title: IMBUS — Project Documentation
text:
1 About this site
This site documents the technical work of the IMBUS project, with a focus on Work Package 2 (Data Standardisation). It covers the DATRAS exchange data format, known data quality issues, the CPUE derivation pipeline, and the data products produced for IMBUS deliverables. It is a living document updated throughout the project.

title: IMBUS — Project Documentation
text:
2 The {obus} R package
The technical implementation of WP2 is the R package {obus} (documentation). {obus} is the software layer that makes the IMBUS data products accessible to end users.
{obus} provides:

Lazy DuckDB access to DATRAS exchange data (HH, HL, CA) stored as Parquet files on a public server, with no download or local storage required.
Pre-computed standardised products — in particular dr_con("HL_standardised"), the core IMBUS D2.3 deliverable: a validated, species-resolved, length-frequency table covering all 29 DATRAS surveys.
Downstream helpers (dr_catch_by_haul(), dr_expand_length()) for zero-filling and swept-area calculations.

The Parquet files served by {obus} are the IMBUS D2.3 integrated data product. The package, the parquet server, and this documentation site together constitute the WP2 technical output.
# Install
remotes::install_github("einarhjorleifsson/obus")

# Example: Atlantic cod length-frequency across all surveys
library(obus)
cod <- dr_con("HL_standardised") |>
  filter(type == "length", latin == "Gadus morhua") |>
  collect()

title: Sampling protocols in DATRAS: StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode
text:
Each DATRAS bottom-trawl survey defines a survey-specific standard species list in its survey manual. Standard species are the commercially important target species for which vessels are required to collect detailed biological data: individual length, weight, sex, maturity, and ideally age. Age-based DATRAS products (CPUEA, IDX) are only available for standard species. The actual species lists are not stored in DATRAS itself — they live in individual survey manuals. What DATRAS does record, for every haul, is which tier of the standard list was active.
Every haul header (HH) record carries two fields that document what the vessel was required to record:








Code
Values
Meaning




StandardSpeciesCode
0 = none, 1 = all standard, 3 = roundfish only, 4 = flatfish only
Which tier of the standard species list was active


BycatchSpeciesCode
0 = none, 1 = open-ended all species, 2 = closed all species, 3 = gadoid only, 4 = flatfish only, 6 = national list
Which additional (bycatch) species were required



These flags control what gets written into the HL table. The formal DATRAS haul-selection rule (NS-IBTS Indices Calculation Procedure, Step II) is:

For a standard species: use only hauls where that species’ tier was active (StandardSpeciesCode ∋ species).
For a bycatch species: use only hauls where bycatch recording was active (BycatchSpeciesCode ≠ 0).
If neither code covers the species: all hauls are eligible.

A species absent from HL may simply not have been required by protocol, not absent from the catch. This distinction matters whenever you zero-fill or compute species-level CPUE.

library(obus)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(Hmisc)

hh <- dr_con("HH")
hl <- dr_con("HL")

2 Empirical standard species lists
There is no universal DATRAS standard species list. Each survey defines its own, and the actual lists are in survey manuals rather than the database. But we can infer them empirically: a species appearing in HL records from hauls where BycatchSpeciesCode = 0 (no bycatch recording) must be on the standard list — there is no other reason it would be recorded.
The table below shows the species appearing in ≥ 5 % of byc = 0 hauls for each survey with at least 10 such hauls. The percentage is the fraction of restricted hauls in which the species was detected; core targets cluster near 100 %.

Survey design is visible in the species list. NS-IBTS targets six gadoid/pelagic species; BTS and DYFS are flatfish surveys; NSSS was designed specifically for sandeel; NL-BSAS monitors juvenile turbots. The Spanish shelf surveys record 30–55 species because they cover deep, species-rich Atlantic and Mediterranean communities where no single target dominates.
The practical consequence: whether a species outside a survey’s standard list is recorded at all depends entirely on BycatchSpeciesCode. Common sole (Solea solea) is standard in BTS and DYFS but bycatch in NS-IBTS; Norway pout is standard in NS-IBTS but bycatch almost everywhere else.

title: Sampling protocols in DATRAS: StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode
section: 3 Species richness as a protocol fingerprint
text:
3 Species richness as a protocol fingerprint
The most direct evidence that these codes matter is species richness: count how many distinct species appear per haul and plot against the protocol flags. No inference needed — the protocol IS the species filter.

spp_per_haul <- hl |>
  filter(NumberAtLength > 0) |>
  group_by(.id) |>
  summarise(n_species = n_distinct(aphia), .groups = "drop")

# Restrict to Q1 (primary quarter for both surveys) across all years
# so seasonal variation doesn't confound the protocol comparison
protocol_richness <- spp_per_haul |>
  inner_join(
    hh |>
      filter(HaulValidity == "V", Quarter == 1,
             Survey %in% c("NS-IBTS", "BITS")) |>
      select(.id, Survey, Year, Quarter, StandardSpeciesCode, BycatchSpeciesCode),
    by = ".id", copy = TRUE
  ) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    std_label = case_when(
      StandardSpeciesCode == "1" ~ "std=1\n(all)",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "3" ~ "std=3\n(roundfish)",
      TRUE ~ paste0("std=", StandardSpeciesCode)
    ),
    byc_label = case_when(
      BycatchSpeciesCode == "0" ~ "byc=0\n(none)",
      BycatchSpeciesCode == "1" ~ "byc=1\n(open)",
      BycatchSpeciesCode == "2" ~ "byc=2\n(closed,\nall)",
      BycatchSpeciesCode == "3" ~ "byc=3\n(gadoid)",
      BycatchSpeciesCode == "4" ~ "byc=4\n(flatfish)",
      TRUE ~ paste0("byc=", BycatchSpeciesCode)
    )
  )

# BITS Q1 — colour by BycatchSpeciesCode to expose the confound
# (most std=3 hauls also have byc=0; most std=1 hauls have byc=1)
p1 <- protocol_richness |>
  filter(Survey == "BITS",
         StandardSpeciesCode %in% c("1", "3"),
         BycatchSpeciesCode   %in% c("0", "1")) |>
  mutate(std_label = factor(std_label, levels = c("std=1\n(all)", "std=3\n(roundfish)")),
         byc_label = factor(byc_label, levels = c("byc=0\n(none)", "byc=1\n(open)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(std_label, n_species, fill = byc_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5, position = position_dodge(0.8)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("byc=0\n(none)" = "#d73027", "byc=1\n(open)" = "#2166ac"),
                    name = "Bycatch code") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Species per haul",
       title = "BITS Q1",
       subtitle = "Bycatch code drives richness; standard list is secondary") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

# NS-IBTS Q1 — BycatchSpeciesCode effect across its full range (std=1 throughout)
p2 <- protocol_richness |>
  filter(Survey == "NS-IBTS", StandardSpeciesCode == "1") |>
  mutate(byc_label = factor(byc_label,
    levels = c("byc=0\n(none)", "byc=3\n(gadoid)", "byc=4\n(flatfish)",
               "byc=2\n(closed,\nall)", "byc=1\n(open)"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(byc_label, n_species, fill = byc_label)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdYlBu", direction = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "NS-IBTS Q1 (std=1)",
       subtitle = "Open bycatch list records 3× more species than no bycatch list") +
  theme_bw()

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)








The bycatch recording code is the dominant driver. In BITS (Q1), the grouped boxplot reveals the confound: almost all std=3 hauls also have no bycatch recording (byc=0, red), while std=1 hauls predominantly have open bycatch recording (byc=1, blue). Within each bycatch code, the standard species list makes little additional difference. In NS-IBTS (Q1), where the standard code is uniformly 1, open bycatch recording (byc=1) yields a median of roughly 14 species per haul; restricting to gadoids drops it to ~5; no bycatch recording to ~4. The NS-IBTS variation is confined to the pre-1990 era, when Denmark, France, and the Soviet Union had not yet adopted the open bycatch protocol. These are not ecological signals — they are recording artefacts.

title: Sampling protocols in DATRAS: StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode
section: 4 Where does the variation come from?
text:
4 Where does the variation come from?
Protocol variation is almost entirely a country × era effect: each participating nation sets its own sampling protocol, and protocols change as surveys harmonise over time. Within a country, the Platform (research vessel) can introduce a secondary split — different vessels operated by different institutions may follow different national protocols, so a survey leg can contain hauls from two vessels with incompatible recording schemes.

# Build per-haul protocol labels for all valid hauls
proto_all <- hh |>
  filter(HaulValidity == "V") |>
  select(Survey, Quarter, Country, Platform, Year,
         StandardSpeciesCode, BycatchSpeciesCode) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    sq_label = paste0(Survey, " Q", Quarter),
    protocol = case_when(
      StandardSpeciesCode == "1" & BycatchSpeciesCode == "1" ~ "full",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "1" & BycatchSpeciesCode == "0" ~ "std=1/byc=0",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "3" & BycatchSpeciesCode == "0" ~ "std=3/byc=0",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "3" & BycatchSpeciesCode == "1" ~ "std=3/byc=1",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "4" & BycatchSpeciesCode == "0" ~ "std=4/byc=0",
      StandardSpeciesCode == "0"                             ~ "std=0",
      TRUE ~ paste0("std=", StandardSpeciesCode, "/byc=", BycatchSpeciesCode)
    )
  )

# Survey-quarters with more than one protocol
sq_vary <- proto_all |>
  group_by(sq_label) |>
  summarise(n_proto = n_distinct(protocol), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_proto > 1) |>
  pull(sq_label)

# Countries where ANY year has within-country platform protocol disagreement
# → those expand to Country/Platform rows; others collapse to Country
mixed_ctry <- proto_all |>
  filter(sq_label %in% sq_vary) |>
  group_by(sq_label, Country, Year) |>
  summarise(n_proto = n_distinct(protocol), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(sq_label, Country) |>
  summarise(ever_mixed = any(n_proto > 1), .groups = "drop")

plat_tile <- proto_all |>
  filter(sq_label %in% sq_vary) |>
  left_join(mixed_ctry, by = c("sq_label", "Country")) |>
  mutate(y_label = if_else(coalesce(ever_mixed, FALSE),
                           paste0(Country, "/", Platform),
                           Country)) |>
  group_by(sq_label, y_label, Year) |>
  summarise(
    dominant = { t <- table(protocol); names(t)[which.max(t)] },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

proto_colours <- c(
  # std=1 (all standard species) — Blues, dark→pale = more→less bycatch coverage
  "full"        = "#08519c",  # std=1 + byc=1 open (most complete)
  "std=1/byc=2" = "#2171b5",  # std=1 + byc=2 closed-list
  "std=1/byc=6" = "#6baed6",  # std=1 + byc=6 national list
  "std=1/byc=4" = "#9ecae1",  # std=1 + byc=4 flatfish only
  "std=1/byc=3" = "#c6dbef",  # std=1 + byc=3 gadoid only
  "std=1/byc=5" = "#c6dbef",  # std=1 + byc=5 (1 haul, same shade as byc=3)
  "std=1/byc=0" = "#deebf7",  # std=1 + byc=0 none (palest)
  # std=3 (roundfish only) — Oranges, dark→light = less→more bycatch coverage
  "std=3/byc=0" = "#d94801",  # roundfish + no bycatch (most restrictive)
  "std=3/byc=1" = "#fdae61",  # roundfish + open bycatch
  # std=4 (flatfish only) — Purples
  "std=4/byc=0" = "#6a51a3",  # flatfish + no bycatch
  "std=4/byc=1" = "#9e9ac8",  # flatfish + open bycatch (rare)
  # no standard list at all
  "std=0"       = "#969696"
)

# Order survey-quarters: major multi-country surveys first
sq_order <- plat_tile |>
  group_by(sq_label) |>
  summarise(n_y = n_distinct(y_label), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n_y)) |>
  pull(sq_label)

plat_tile <- plat_tile |>
  mutate(
    sq_label = factor(sq_label, levels = rev(sq_order)),
    dominant = factor(dominant, levels = names(proto_colours))
  )

# facet_grid with space = "free_y" gives each panel height proportional
# to its number of y-axis values — no extra packages required
ggplot(plat_tile, aes(Year, y_label, fill = dominant)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Protocol", values = proto_colours,
                    na.value = "grey90", drop = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 5)) +
  facet_grid(sq_label ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Dominant sampling protocol by platform and year",
       subtitle = paste0("Country/Platform shown only where vessels within a country disagreed;",
                         " otherwise collapsed to Country")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text     = element_text(size = 7),
    strip.text.y    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 7, angle = 0),
    axis.text.y     = element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text.x     = element_text(size = 7),
    panel.spacing   = unit(0.3, "lines")
  )








Several patterns stand out:

Poland (PL) in BITS ran without bycatch recording until 2009, alternating between full (std=1) and roundfish-only (std=3) standard lists throughout that period. Two vessels operated simultaneously with different protocols in some years (PL/AA36 vs PL/67BC).
Russia (RU) joined BITS with std=3+byc=0 in 2009, then switched to full protocol.
Germany (DE) in BITS: vessel DE/06JR ran std=3 from 1993–1998 while DE/06SL ran full protocol in the same years; DE/06S1 also used std=3 in 2001–2002 before switching. Different vessels from the same country thus operated under different protocols within the same survey year.
NS-IBTS Q1 variation is confined to the 1970s–1980s, when Denmark (DK/…), France (FR/…), and the Soviet Union (SUHH) had not yet adopted the open bycatch protocol.
Can-Mar Q3 uses byc=6 — a Canadian national bycatch code outside the standard DATRAS classification.
NSSS Q4 has GB-SCT operating with std=0/byc=0 (no standard or bycatch list), meaning the Scottish component of this survey contributes no species information to the standard HL record.
From ~2010 onward BITS converges to full protocol across all participating countries.

title: Sampling protocols in DATRAS: StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode
section: 5 Common sole in BITS: a bycatch species with a paper trail

title: Sampling protocols in DATRAS: StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode
text:
6 Filtering in practice
Before zero-filling or computing species-level CPUE, exclude hauls where recording was incomplete. The protocol flags are available in both HH and in any downstream product that carries them (e.g. dr_HL_standardised() from the obus package):

# Protocol flags live in HH — filter there before calling dr_HL_standardised()
complete_hh <- hh |>
  filter(StandardSpeciesCode == "1",   # full standard list
         BycatchSpeciesCode  != "0")   # some bycatch recording

# Pass filtered HH into dr_HL_standardised() so only protocol-complete hauls
# are included; join back to HH on .id if you need the flags downstream
hl_std <- dr_HL_standardised(complete_hh, hl)

Note that filtering to StandardSpeciesCode == "1" alone is not sufficient for bycatch species: a haul with std=1 but byc=0 records all standard species but nothing outside that list. For flatfish like common sole, which appear on the standard list in some surveys but are bycatch in others, checking both codes is essential.

title: CPUE derivation: CPUEL product vs HL-derived
text:
ICES provides a pre-computed CPUE-by-length product (CPUEL) for a subset of DATRAS surveys. This document compares it against CPUE derived directly from the raw HH and HL tables and identifies three structural problems with the CPUEL product.
Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua, AphiaID 126436) is used as a concrete species throughout. The structural findings apply across species.

title: CPUE derivation: CPUEL product vs HL-derived
CPUE derivation: CPUEL product vs HL-derived
text:
3 Historical reference: dr_cpue_length()

Note: dr_cpue_length() is superseded by the dr_HL_standardised() pipeline. The function below is preserved as documentation of how the derivation works.

The three problems documented below all stem from using the CPUEL product. An earlier recommended alternative was to derive CPUE directly from HH and HL using the dr_cpue_length() helper below. The function:

Uses the full .id haul key (Survey:Year:Quarter:Country:Platform:Gear:StationName:HaulNumber), avoiding the ambiguity of CPUEL’s shortened key.
Zero-fills via HH |> left_join(HL), so every valid haul appears in the output — hauls with no catch for the target species get length_mm = 0, n_haul = 0, n_hour = 0.
Outputs the minimum necessary columns: .id, length_mm, n_haul, n_hour. Haul metadata (position, gear, date, etc.) is retrieved by joining the output to dr_con("HH") on .id.
Works lazily within the dplyr/DuckDB framework — call collect() on the result when ready to pull into memory.


#' Derive length-frequency CPUE from HH and HL
#'
#' @param hh  Lazy HH table, pre-filtered to the target survey/year/quarter
#'            and restricted to valid hauls (HaulValidity == "V").
#' @param hl  Lazy HL table, pre-filtered to a single target species
#'            (e.g. filter(aphia == 126436)).
#' @param collapse_sex   If TRUE (default), sum across sex levels.
#'            Set FALSE to retain sex as a grouping dimension.
#' @param collapse_stage If TRUE (default), sum across DevelopmentStage levels.
#'            Set FALSE to retain developmental stage as a grouping dimension.
#'
#' @return A lazy dplyr/DuckDB table with columns:
#'   .id, length_mm, [sex], [DevelopmentStage], n_haul, n_hour.
#'   Zero-catch hauls appear as a single row with length_mm = 0, n_haul = 0,
#'   n_hour = 0. Join to dr_con("HH") on .id to retrieve haul metadata.
dr_cpue_length <- function(hh, hl,
                           collapse_sex   = TRUE,
                           collapse_stage = TRUE) {
  group_vars <- c(".id", "length_mm")
  if (!collapse_sex)   group_vars <- c(group_vars, "sex")
  if (!collapse_stage) group_vars <- c(group_vars, "DevelopmentStage")

  hh |>
    select(.id, HaulDuration, DataType) |>
    left_join(
      hl |>
        dr_add_length_mm() |>
        select(.id, length_mm, sex, DevelopmentStage,
               NumberAtLength, SubsamplingFactor),
      by = ".id"
    ) |>
    dr_add_n_and_cpue() |>
    group_by(across(all_of(group_vars))) |>
    summarise(
      n_haul = sum(n_haul, na.rm = TRUE),
      n_hour = sum(n_hour, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      length_mm = coalesce(length_mm, 0),
      n_haul    = coalesce(n_haul,    0),
      n_hour    = coalesce(n_hour,    0)
    )
}

5 Problem 1 — Ambiguous haul key
The CPUEL output uses a shortened haul key — Survey:Year:Quarter:Platform:Gear:HaulNumber — omitting Country and StationName. The full key used in HH and HL is Survey:Year:Quarter:Country:Platform:Gear:StationName:HaulNumber. Problem

Ambiguous haul key
CPUEL omits Country and StationName from the output key. 2,400+ short keys resolve to multiple full hauls in HH. Joining CPUEL to HH for metadata retrieval is unreliable for those hauls.

title: CPUEL: emulation and validation
text: This document asks: can we reconstruct CPUEL row-by-row from raw HH and HL tables? compute_cpue_emulation() does this and is validated here across all 17 Survey-Quarter combinations and all available years. The goal is to understand what CPUEL computes internally and to attribute row-count and CPUE discrepancies to their specific causes.

1.3.1 Cause 1 — Short-key haul collapsing (emulation < CPUEL)

Fisheries-independent bottom trawl surveys are conducted annually under the EU Data Collection Framework. Beyond their traditional role in informing catch advice, these data are increasingly used for ecosystem assessments, climate change tracking, and biodiversity monitoring. Access: Accessing and merging the data requires a high level of technical skill. Non-scientific users (Advisory Councils, fisheries organizations, NGOs, managers) find the data largely out of reach.

title: IMBUS Project Overview
text:
Fisheries-independent bottom trawl surveys are conducted annually under the EU Data Collection Framework. Beyond their traditional role in informing catch advice, these data are increasingly used for ecosystem assessments, climate change tracking, and biodiversity monitoring. However, their broader use is hampered by two problems:

Access: Accessing and merging the data requires a high level of technical skill. Non-scientific users (Advisory Councils, fisheries organizations, NGOs, managers) find the data largely out of reach.
Quality: Quality control has historically been post-operational — months after data collection, often too late to correct errors at source.

IMBUS addresses both problems through standardized tools and improved on-vessel quality assurance.

text:
1 Executive Summary
This document is the technical specification for the IMBUS integrated data product (D2.3, Type: DATA). It defines the proposed column names, file formats, data tier structure, and design principles for the standardised representation of the ICES DATRAS bottom trawl survey exchange tables.
The D2.3 product itself — the parquet files — is hosted at https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/ (interim; transfer to the ICES open access portal is planned under D2.4). Long-term sustainability is handled by WP5: D5.3 (ICES, M18) formally integrates the IMBUS data products and the {obus} codebase into the ICES DATRAS R library and ICES web services. The raw DATRAS data supply that feeds D2.3 is formalised in D5.1 (ICES, M6).
The principal design decisions are:

Unified column naming. A single, consistent set of column names is applied across all record types and surveys, regardless of API source or era. The full field mapping is documented in D2.2 §2.
Parquet-based distribution. HH, HL, and CA exchange tables are stored as columnar parquet files enabling fast, column-selective querying without full downloads.
Sentinel value removal. The DATRAS convention of using −9 for missing values is replaced with proper missing-value encoding.
Species resolution via WoRMS AphiaID. Historical species codes (ITIS TSN, NODC) are mapped to current WoRMS AphiaIDs for cross-era joins.
Unique haul identifiers. An 8-field composite key (.id) uniquely identifies each haul across all surveys, years, and countries.
A standardised HL product. A unified standardised representation of the HL exchange table — HL_standardised.parquet — resolves the unit ambiguities, DataType dependencies, and sex-recording heterogeneity of raw HL into a single clean, self-contained product covering all valid hauls across all 29 surveys.
DataType-corrected CPUE. A transparent, reproducible calculation pathway raises raw exchange data to catch-per-unit-effort, handling all DataType variants correctly.

The specification is implemented in the R package {obus} (https://github.com/einarhjorleifsson/obus). {obus} is explicitly experimental and serves as the proof-of-concept implementation for the WP2 period; its functionality is intended to be upstreamed into the official icesDatras R package under WP5/D5.3 (M18).

title: D2.3 — IMBUS Integrated Data Product Specification
text:
2 Background and Purpose
This document is the technical specification for D2.3, the IMBUS integrated data product. It should be read alongside D2.2 (Data Formats and Metadata), which provides the field-by-field documentation of the current DATRAS exchange format — the reference for the naming conventions, field descriptions, and known issues that underpin the design decisions here.
The IMBUS project (Sep 2025 – Aug 2027) is a 24-month EU-funded initiative to improve use of ICES trawl survey data. WP2 is responsible for data standardisation. The four WP2 objectives are:

Assess user requirements. (Addressed in D2.1, April 2026.)
Develop a data format for WP3–5 products.
Generate meta-data descriptions.
Process current DATRAS data into the new format.

D2.3 delivers on objectives 2 and 4 — the standardised data product. D2.2 delivers objective 3 — the metadata documentation.

2.1 Scope
In scope:

Proposed standardised column names and their mapping from current DATRAS names.
Parquet file format, hosting, and access via the {obus} R package.
Unique haul identifier (.id) construction.
Design and schema of the standardised HL product (HL_standardised).
Data tier structure (Tier 0 raw / Tier 1 standardised).
Calculation pathways from raw exchange data to CPUE-by-length and exploratory CPUE-by-age.
{obus} interim status and transition path to icesDatras (D5.3).

Out of scope:

Field-by-field documentation of the current DATRAS exchange format — see D2.2.
Official CPUEA and age-based survey indices (ICES Datacenter products).
Deployment to the ICES open access portal — subject of D2.4.
Per-survey metadata fact sheets — addressed separately under user requirement UR-Q1.

title: D2.3 — IMBUS Integrated Data Product Specification
section: 3 IMBUS Proposed Data Formats — D2.3 Product Specification
text:
3 IMBUS Proposed Data Formats — D2.3 Product Specification

Deliverable D2.3 scope. This document is the technical specification for the IMBUS integrated data product (D2.3, Type: DATA, due M12). It defines the proposed column names, file formats, data tier structure, and design principles. The D2.3 product itself — the parquet files — will be hosted on the ICES open access portal under D2.4 (M12). The current interim location is https://heima.hafro.is/~einarhj/datras/.
Long-term sustainability is handled by WP5: D5.3 (ICES, M18) formally integrates the IMBUS data products and the {obus} codebase into the ICES DATRAS R library and ICES web services, ensuring D2.3 has an institutional home beyond the project period. The raw DATRAS data supply that feeds D2.3 is formalised in D5.1 (ICES, M6).


3.1 Standardised Data Formats

3.1.1 Harmonised variables
The IMBUS product uses standard column names throughout (see D2.2 — Current Issues: column naming). Where data originate from the legacy XML API, an automatic translation step maps legacy to standard names using the field dictionary dr_lookup_fields. Fields with no standard equivalent retain their original names. The full mapping (~292 fields) is available in the dr_lookup_fields data object in {obus} and in the companion DATRAS Field Reference.

Interim names. Two fields — sex and aphia — use IMBUS canonical names that deviate from the (inconsistent) ICES “new” names, as a temporary measure pending resolution by the ICES Datacenter. See D2.2 — IMBUS interim canonical names.

Additional standardisation steps applied to all exchange tables:

Sentinel value removal. The DATRAS convention of using −9 for missing values is replaced with proper missing-value encoding (NA).
Species resolution. Historical species codes (ITIS TSN, NODC) are mapped to current WoRMS AphiaIDs (aphia) for cross-era joins.
Unique haul identifier. An 8-field composite key (.id) uniquely identifies each haul across all surveys, years, and countries.



3.1.2 Unique Haul Identifier
A composite key constructed from eight fields uniquely identifies each haul:
.id = Survey : Year : Quarter : Country : Platform : Gear : StationName : HaulNumber
Example: "NS-IBTS:2023:1:NL:58G2:GOV:18:27"
This is the recommended join key for all operations across the IMBUS product suite. A shorter 6-field key (omitting Country and StationName) is also available for comparison with the ICES CPUEL derived product, which omits those two fields. The 6-field key is ambiguous — more than 2,400 short keys match more than one haul in the full dataset — and is provided only for backward-compatibility diagnostics, not for production use.


3.1.3 The standardised HL product: design rationale
The raw DATRAS HL exchange table mixes three distinct kinds of information in every row: length-frequency measurements, haul-level totals, and subsampling metadata. On top of this, several field values cannot be interpreted without context from other fields or from a separate table: the length unit depends on a code field (LengthCode); the meaning of a count depends on the haul’s DataType and HaulDuration (both in HH, not HL); and species are identified by numeric code rather than name. The result is that every analyst must re-derive units, joins, and scaling from scratch before any analysis can begin.
The IMBUS standardised HL product resolves these ambiguities once, producing a clean, self-contained table where every column has a single unambiguous meaning. Four design decisions shape the result.
Two counting paths, one table. The HL table contains two independent records of the same catch: length-frequency measurements (NumberAtLength) and haul-level totals (TotalNumber). Both are scaled to consistent units — numbers per haul (n_haul) and numbers per hour of towing (n_hour) — and retained in a single table, distinguished by a type column:

type = "length" — counts derived from NumberAtLength, one row per species × length class per haul. Used for length-structured analyses: length-frequency distributions, age-length keys, year-class tracking.
type = "haul" — counts derived from TotalNumber, one row per species per haul. Used for haul-level totals, biomass indices, and as a cross-check on the length-derived totals.

Keeping both paths in a single table, rather than two separate files, means every caught species is always present (via its type = "haul" row) even when it was never individually measured at length. The type flag makes the distinction explicit: any downstream analysis using n_haul or n_hour must filter on type first.
Sex as a proportion. Raw HL records the same haul × species × length class in multiple rows split by sex. Rather than carrying sex as a row-splitting dimension, the standardised product collapses sex into a single derived column p_females — the proportion of individually sexed fish at each length class that were female. Female and male counts can be recovered by multiplying n_haul or n_hour by p_females and 1 − p_females respectively. p_females is absent when no fish in the group were individually sexed.
DevelopmentStage dropped. Across the 2010–2020 exchange data, 99.7% of records carry no developmental stage code; the remainder are summed over during aggregation in any case. Users who need to work with developmental stage should access the raw HL parquet directly.
StandardSpeciesCode / BycatchSpeciesCode not carried through. These haul-level flags from HH record what a vessel was obligated to report for each haul. They are not carried into the standardised product but remain available via a join to HH on .id.


3.1.4 Summary: proposed data tiers
Tier 0 — Raw exchange parquets (hosted)
  HH.parquet, HL.parquet, CA.parquet, LT.parquet
  All original submission fields; standard names applied on fetch; −9 → NA.
  For: expert users, QC, full-fidelity reproduction.

Tier 1 — Standardised HL product (hosted)
  HL_standardised.parquet   Unified type="length" + type="haul" rows; valid hauls only.
                            Generated by: dr_HL_standardised(dr_con("HH"), dr_con("HL"),
                                                             haulval = "V")
                            Accessed via: dr_con("HL_standardised")
  For: all survey-analysis users; the recommended starting point for CPUE, indices,
       length distributions, and biomass workflows.

Official ICES derived products (accessible via dr_get())
  CPUEA / IDX   Age-based CPUE and indices; ICES Datacenter products.
  For: formal stock assessment; not produced by IMBUS.




3.2 File Formats Used

3.2.1 Parquet
The IMBUS product distributes HH, HL, CA, and the standardised HL as columnar parquet files. Parquet enables fast, column-selective querying without downloading the full table — a critical advantage given that HL alone contains tens of millions of rows across all surveys and years.

These files are readable by any tool that supports the parquet format or the DuckDB query engine: R, Python, Julia, DBeaver, and others.


3.2.2 Data access via {obus}
The {obus} R package provides two access modes:
Lazy parquet connection (recommended for large queries). A connection to a parquet file returns a lazy query object. Filters are pushed down to the file; only the requested rows and columns are transferred into memory:
library(obus)
library(dplyr)

# Length-frequency CPUE — filter to length rows and desired species/survey
cod_lengths <- dr_con("HL_standardised") |>
  filter(type == "length", Survey == "NS-IBTS", latin == "Gadus morhua") |>
  collect()

# Haul-level catch totals
cod_hauls <- dr_con("HL_standardised") |>
  filter(type == "haul", Survey == "NS-IBTS", latin == "Gadus morhua") |>
  collect()
Full download via dr_get(). Downloads and collects an entire table into memory, optionally filtered via the legacy ICES XML API. Appropriate for smaller, targeted queries.


3.2.3 {obus}: interim status and transition path
{obus} is explicitly experimental (lifecycle status: experimental) and is best understood as the proof-of-concept implementation for the WP2 data standardisation work. It is not intended to be a permanent, standalone R package. Its role within the IMBUS project lifecycle is:

Proof-of-concept. Provide a working, validated implementation of the naming conventions, DataType arithmetic, parquet access, and CPUE pathways described in this document during the WP2 delivery period (M1–M12).
D2.3 delivery vehicle. Serve as the primary means of accessing the D2.3 data product (parquet files) while those files are hosted on the interim server.
Design feedback loop. Accumulate community experience and feedback that directly informs what is worth upstreaming into the official ICES infrastructure.

{obus} builds on, rather than replaces, the official icesDatras package — it imports icesDatras and delegates XML-source downloads to it. The added value is the parquet/DuckDB access layer, unified column naming, DataType-aware derived fields, and the quality-check family.
Intended trajectory. Under WP5/D5.3 (ICES, M18), the functionality proven in {obus} is a candidate for integration into the official ICES DATRAS R library (icesDatras), alongside migration of the parquet files to ICES-managed infrastructure. The naming-convention mapping, the DataType arithmetic, and the composite haul key (.id) are the most transferable elements.




3.3 Updated Meta-data Descriptions
The IMBUS standard names and field definitions described in D2.2 §2 and this document constitute an updated meta-data description for the DATRAS exchange tables. The companion document DATRAS Field Reference provides complete field reference tables for all HH, HL, CA, and LT fields, including types, units, valid values, and a drop-or-derive quick reference.
Per-survey meta-data fact sheets (coverage, gear history, time-series breaks, QC history) are not produced by D2.3. These are addressed separately under user requirement UR-Q1.



3.4 Standardised Code for Processing DATRAS Data
WP2 does not generate new CPUE data series. Instead, it provides transparent, reproducible code that any user can apply to the standardised exchange tables to generate CPUE on demand.

3.4.1 Data flow
DATRAS database
      │
      ▼
Raw exchange download    ← getDATRAS() (legacy XML API)
      │
      ▼
Type normalisation       ← dr_settypes(): column types enforced; −9 → NA
Column renaming          ← dr_translate(): legacy → standard names
      │
      ▼
Raw parquets (server)    ← HH.parquet / HL.parquet / CA.parquet
      │
      ▼
Standardised HL          ← dr_HL_standardised(dr_con("HH"), dr_con("HL"), haulval="V")
  (server)               ← HL_standardised.parquet
      │
      ▼
User analysis            ← dr_con("HL_standardised") |> filter(type == ...) |> collect()
                         → dr_catch_by_haul() / dr_expand_length() for zero-filling
Stages 1–3 are handled once by the data provider (currently Einar Hjörleifsson; ICES from D2.4/D5.3). The standardised HL is regenerated whenever the raw parquets are updated. Users interact from stage 4 onward.

3.4.3 CPUE calculation pathway
CPUE-by-length requires five steps:

Filter valid hauls: retain only hauls with HaulValidity = "V". (Pre-applied in HL_standardised.)
Filter standard species records: retain SpeciesValidity = "1".
Join DataType and HaulDuration from HH to HL on .id. (Pre-applied.)
Compute n_haul and n_hour using the DataType-appropriate formula. (Pre-applied.)
Aggregate across sex and species category. (Pre-applied; sex summarised as p_females.)

For users working from dr_con("HL_standardised"), steps 1, 3, 4, and 5 are already complete. The remaining user step is to filter SpeciesValidity = "1" and select the survey, species, and year range of interest.
The DataType-aware arithmetic that underpins step 4 handles the three submission conventions:

HaulDuration is in minutes throughout. CPUE = catch in numbers per one hour of towing.


3.4.4 Zero observations and zero-fill
A CPUE value of zero means the species was absent from that haul but was caught by at least one vessel in the same survey × year × quarter. Zero rows are required for unbiased abundance indices: when aggregating CPUE across hauls within a stratum, hauls where the species was not observed must contribute a zero — omitting them inflates the mean.
HL_standardised contains only observed rows (no zeros). Zero-filling is applied downstream by dr_catch_by_haul() and dr_expand_length(), which add an explicit zero row for every haul in a Survey × Year × Quarter where a given species was absent. This matches the convention used by the official ICES CPUE data products.
A note on phantom zeros. The pooled zero-fill approach can produce phantom zeros for hauls that were never required to record a given species. The DATRAS HH table records what each vessel was obligated to report (StandardSpeciesCode, BycatchSpeciesCode), and the official ICES index methodology uses these flags for a further haul-selection step. The {obus} zero-fill functions follow the DATRAS CPUE product convention and do not implement this additional filter. Users building formal survey indices should apply haul-selection using the HH flags directly.

Step 1 is directly satisfied by dr_con("HL_standardised"), substantially reducing the entry barrier for this approach.
A pre-computed CA_raised.parquet product (one row per .id × aphia × age) has been proposed as a complement to HL_standardised. Its design requires input from WP4 on ALK pooling level, plus-group threshold, and area-pooled CA rows; see Appendix 2 for the current schema sketch.

title: D2.3 — IMBUS Integrated Data Product Specification
text:
4 Discussion and Conclusions
The D2.3 product specification addresses a long-standing barrier to broader use of ICES bottom trawl survey data: the complexity of deriving analysis-ready products from the raw DATRAS exchange format. The raw format is rich and flexible — necessarily so, to accommodate the diversity of national sampling protocols across 29 surveys — but that same flexibility imposes a substantial entry cost on users who simply want species-level catch-per-unit-effort for a given survey and year. Every analyst has historically had to resolve unit ambiguities, handle DataType-conditional arithmetic, and manage zero-filling independently, with no assurance of consistency across research groups.
A single standardised product for the majority of use cases. The HL_standardised parquet delivers what most users need in one file: DataType-corrected counts at length and at the haul level, species names resolved, lengths in a single consistent unit, and sex summarised in a recoverable form. The type column cleanly separates the two counting paths that raw HL conflates, so users working with length distributions filter to type = "length", while users working with haul totals or biomass filter to type = "haul" — without needing to understand the underlying DataType conventions or subsampling arithmetic.
Coverage and quality are substantially improved relative to the ICES CPUEL product. The official CPUEL product covers 8 of 29 surveys and does not apply a haul-validity filter. HL_standardised covers all 29 surveys, filters to valid hauls, and provides an unambiguous 8-field join key. For the 8 surveys where CPUEL exists, WP2’s analysis confirmed that the HL_standardised CPUE series are consistent with CPUEL (modulo the known structural differences), validating the derivation.
The design makes an implicit contract explicit. The raw HL table contains two independent records of the same catch — length-frequency measurements and haul-level totals — mixed in the same rows without any formal distinction. The standardised product separates these into two row types with consistent column names and units. When the two paths agree, users can proceed with confidence; a persistent divergence points to a genuine data inconsistency in the original submission, flagged by the dr_check_totalno() quality function.
Known limitations. Three open items require acknowledgement. First, the zero-fill convention — pooling species across all hauls in a survey × year × quarter — matches the DATRAS CPUE product convention but can produce phantom zeros for hauls never required to record a given species. Formal index calculations should apply the additional haul-selection step using the StandardSpeciesCode and BycatchSpeciesCode flags in HH. Second, the pre-computed CA_raised product (age-disaggregated abundance) has not been produced; its design depends on WP4 input on ALK pooling conventions that has not yet been finalised. Third, the parquet files remain on an interim personal server; transfer to ICES-managed infrastructure is pending D2.4 and D5.3.
Sustainability and reproducibility. HL_standardised is derived from the raw exchange parquets using a single documented function call (dr_HL_standardised()). Any user can reproduce the product from the Tier 0 parquets using open code, without any intermediate files. The {obus} package is explicitly experimental; its functionality, together with the parquet files, is a candidate for integration into the official icesDatras R package and ICES-managed infrastructure under WP5/D5.3 (M18). At that point the D2.3 products will have an institutional home within ICES that ensures their long-term availability and maintenance.

title: D2.3 — IMBUS Integrated Data Product Specification
text:
5 Further Work
The following items are open as of the date of this document:

Parquet hosting. The current parquet files are on a personal server (heima.hafro.is). Transfer to the ICES open access portal is pending WP5/ICES coordination (D2.4).
Integration into ICES infrastructure (D5.3). Per decisions from the 1 June 2026 IMBUS WP2-WP5 meeting, parquet/DuckDB functionality should be incorporated into the official ICES DATRAS R package rather than maintained as a separate tool. This is formally the scope of WP5 deliverable D5.3 (ICES, M18).
CA_raised product. Age-disaggregated abundance (one row per .id × aphia × age) derived from ALK application to HL_standardised. Design requires input from WP4 on ALK pooling level, plus-group threshold, and area-pooled CA rows. See Appendix 2 for the current schema sketch.
Haul-selection step for formal indices. The phantom-zero limitation described in §Standardised Code for Processing DATRAS Data requires implementing a haul-selection filter using StandardSpeciesCode / BycatchSpeciesCode. This is needed before HL_standardised can serve as a drop-in input for formal survey index calculation.
Area standardisation. Mapping from haul positions to C-squares and ICES statistical divisions is partially implemented (dr_assign_area()) but the lookup helpers are not yet complete in {obus}.

title: IMBUS WP2–WP5 Meeting — Minutes
section: 2.1 2.1 Scope and Objective of Work Package 2
text:
2.1 2.1 Scope and Objective of Work Package 2
A significant portion of the meeting was dedicated to clarifying what WP2 is actually required to produce. Key points of discussion included:

WP2 so far focused exclusively on submitted (Exchange) data, not on derived data products such as CPUE data. The grant agreement does not mention the CPUE product.
The core objective of WP2 is to standardise the metadata structure and schema of the submitted DATRAS exchange data to produce a generalised, flat-file representation of the HH, HL and CA hierarchy that removes hidden complexity and lookup dependencies.
The output of WP2 is primarily a data format specification and metadata description document, not necessarily a fully-deployed data product, though illustrative code should accompany it.
A key value-added highlighted by Vaishav is bringing all fragmented metadata descriptions under one umbrella, making the data accessible to new users without expert knowledge.

title: IMBUS WP2–WP5 Meeting — Minutes
section: 2.2 2.2 Data Structure and Known User Challenges
text:
2.2 2.2 Data Structure and Known User Challenges
Vaishav Soni identified several structural issues that WP2 should address to improve usability of the Exchange format:

Users frequently struggle to understand the hierarchical relationship between HH (haul header), HL (length data) and CA (catch-at-age) tables. A unified, relational mapping would resolve this.
Field descriptions and metadata are not bundled with the download – users must navigate to a separate link. Including field-level descriptions in the data schema would be a significant improvement.
Several fields contain hidden calculations or rely on implicit rules that are not documented (e.g. CatCatchWeight is defined by a combination of sex, maturity, length class, development stage and length measurement type).
Area standardisation is a known gap: survey area codes vary across surveys, and a mapping to ICES statistical rectangles, C-squares or ICES divisions is needed.
Length unit inconsistencies (centimetres vs. millimetres) and sub-sampling factors require explicit handling and documentation.
Data type flags in HH (e.g. DataType = ‘C’) do not always align with duration fields, creating subtle interpretation errors.

title: IMBUS WP2–WP5 Meeting — Minutes
section: 2.3 2.3 CPUE Data Products – Scope and Limitations
text:
2.3 2.3 CPUE Data Products – Scope and Limitations
The meeting explored whether CPUE-by-length or CPUE-by-age products should be within WP2 scope:

CPUE-by-length is available in DATRAS for a limited set of surveys (IBTS North Sea, Baltic BTS, French survey). Extending this to all surveys is the longer-term plan, but is outside current WP2 resources.
CPUE-by-age requires a full age-slicing procedure that varies by survey and country – this was collectively agreed to be out of scope for WP2.
WP2 should, however, describe the standardisation steps needed to reach CPUE-by-length from raw Exchange data, in a way that other work packages and users can use.
The data volume challenge of CPUE products was noted: CPUE-by-length generates large zero-expanded tables and would strain the DATRAS data warehouse if extended to all surveys. A code/script-based approach is preferred over maintaining a static data product.

title: IMBUS WP2–WP5 Meeting — Minutes
text:
2.4 2.4 Data Access and Technical Infrastructure

Einar referenced the faster data download mechanism for DATRAS exchange data that has been implemented by Vaishav. He has been experimenting with (CSV/parquet-based, via DuckDB), noting it substantially outperforms the existing XML-based ICES-DATRAS R package for large queries.
Vaishav identified that the CSV-format download script has already been published on the ICES GitHub. It has apparently been added without his explicit authorisation and not yet up to date. The group agreed this should be moved to a development/test environment rather than left in production.
The agreed direction is that the ICES DATRAS data package should be the canonical source for data download and processing. Future enhancements – including Einar’s faster CSV/parquet mechanism – should be integrated into this package as an optional output format.
Einar advocated for intermediate data steps being exposed to users, not just final outputs. A key design principle is that users who want to dig into the data processing should have access to intermediate tidy data frames, not just plots or final indices.

title: IMBUS WP2–WP5 Meeting — Minutes
section: 2.5 2.5 Link to FishMap and the September Workshop
text:
2.5 2.5 Link to FishMap and the September Workshop
Martin Pastoors reported on a recent meeting with the FishMap project (Thomas Mildenberger, DTU). While there is partial overlap in spatial mapping of survey data, the approaches differ: IMBUS focuses on the data provenance and format coming out of the survey pipeline, whereas FishMap takes exchange data as-is and applies its own corrections. The planned joint workshop in early September was agreed as a key milestone, with the expectation that by then IMBUS has a clear, documented outline of the WP2 data flow from the DATRAS database to downstream users, including the link with the ICES Secretariat.

title: DATRAS R Package — Data Checks and Processing
text:
1 Overview
The {DATRAS} R package (Kristensen & Jardim) was developed independently of and prior to the IMBUS project. It is not an IMBUS deliverable. This page reviews it purely as prior art — to understand what data checks and transformations were already established, and to inform the design of WP2 standardisation work and the {obus} proof-of-concept package.
{DATRAS} provides tools for reading, subsetting, and analysing ICES DATRAS exchange data. Its core data structure is the DATRASraw object — a named list of three data frames (CA, HH, HL) with a shared haul.id factor linking records across tables.
The notes below document the data checks, transformations, and integrity tests performed during reading and processing in R/read_datras.R.

title: DATRAS R Package — Data Checks and Processing
text:
2 Data ingestion
Data enter via two routes:

getDatrasExchange() — downloads directly from the ICES web service using icesDatras::getDATRAS().
readICES() / readExchange() — reads from a flat CSV exchange file (or a .zip of one).

Both routes pass through the same normalisation pipeline described below.

3 Normalisation pipeline

3.1 1. Missing value replacement (minus9toNA)
DATRAS uses −9 as a sentinel for missing values in numeric fields. The function minus9toNA() scans every numeric column in all three tables and replaces exact occurrences of −9 (within floating-point tolerance 1e-14) with NA.
is9 <- which(abs(x[[i]][, ii] + 9) < 1e-14)
if (length(is9) > 0) x[[i]][, ii][is9] <- NA






Note



The tolerance test rather than exact equality (== -9) guards against floating-point representation artefacts introduced during CSV parsing.




3.2 2. Column name harmonisation (renameDATRAS)

Capitalise first letter of every column name (handles inconsistencies across exchange file versions).

The {obus} package and D2.2 propose ValidAphiaID as the canonical name. These two packages are therefore inconsistent on this column name. See open issue in AGENTS.md.

The ICES rectangle field is named StatRec in HH but AreaCode in some older CA submissions. After renaming, if CA$StatRec is absent, it is aliased from CA$AreaCode:

Scientific names are resolved from two internal lookup tables:

The resulting Species column is a factor of scientific names, applied to both HL and CA.






Note



The WoRMS table is a static file bundled with the package; it does not query the live WoRMS API and will drift out of date as taxonomy changes.




4.4 7. Count reconstruction (Count in HL)
A key correction: HLNoAtLngt as submitted to DATRAS is normalised differently depending on DataType. The package reverses this to recover the actual count observed in the haul:

multiplier1 <- ifelse(d3$DataType == "C", d3$HaulDur / 60, 1)
multiplier2 <- ifelse(!is.na(d3$SubFactor), d3$SubFactor, 1)

Note

Important



Relevance for D2.2 / {obus}: The {obus} equivalent is dr_add_n_and_cpue(), which computes n_haul = NumberAtLength × SubsamplingFactor at the individual record level and additionally produces n_hour = n_haul / HaulDuration × 60 as an explicit second output. The two implementations differ in several ways described below.




4.5 Differences between {DATRAS} and {obus} for DataType "R"
Both packages apply the subsampling factor record-by-record, so summed totals per haul agree under normal conditions. The differences arise in edge cases and in what the functions produce.

4.5.1 NA SubFactor / SubsamplingFactor
When the subsampling factor is missing, the two packages diverge immediately:

Both packages substitute 1 for a missing SubFactor / SubsamplingFactor when DataType == "R", reflecting the assumption that absence of a subsampling factor implies the full catch was measured. (The {obus} package was updated to match this behaviour in June 2026; prior to that it propagated NA.)


4.5.2 DataType "P" (pseudocategory sampling)
DataType "P" is not in the DATRAS branching logic. It falls through to the same arithmetic as "R" without any acknowledgement:
# DATRAS — "P" not mentioned; multiplier1 = 1 silently
multiplier1 <- ifelse(d3$DataType == "C", d3$HaulDur / 60, 1)
# {obus} — "P" listed explicitly
n_haul = case_when(
  DataType == "C" ~ NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor * HaulDuration / 60,
  DataType == "R" ~ NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor,
  DataType == "P" ~ NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor,   # explicit
  DataType == "S" ~ NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor,
  DataType == "-9" ~ NA,
  is.na(DataType)  ~ NA,
  TRUE ~ NA
)
The computed value is numerically identical for "P", but {obus} makes the intent explicit and correctly returns NA for "-9" and unknown DataTypes rather than silently computing a number.


4.5.3 Invalid or missing DataType
DataType = "-9" is a character string and is not caught by minus9toNA() (which only processes numeric columns). It therefore survives into the DATRAS count calculation, where ifelse(DataType == "C", ...) evaluates to FALSE and multiplier1 = 1 — a number is produced rather than flagged as invalid:

4.5.4 n_hour not produced by {DATRAS}
The DATRAS package produces only Count (estimated numbers in the haul). Per-hour CPUE is left to the user to compute downstream. {obus} makes it a first-class output:
# {obus} always produces both
n_haul = NumberAtLength * SubsamplingFactor          # numbers in haul
n_hour = n_haul / HaulDuration * 60                 # numbers per hour


4.5.5 Size-stratified subsampling — a note on aggregation
When SubFactor varies within a haul × species group (size-stratified subsampling, documented in D2.2 for GB-SCT and DK under DataType "P" and "R"), both packages compute correctly at the record level. The risk is not in the per-row multiplication but in any downstream workflow that assumes a single uniform SubFactor per group — for example, extracting SubFactor from the first record and multiplying by a summed HLNoAtLngt. Neither package protects against that misuse, but it is a more common error pattern with the DATRAS Count column (which masks the original HLNoAtLngt and SubFactor individually) than with {obus}, where both NumberAtLength and SubsamplingFactor remain visible.

title: DATRAS R Package — Data Checks and Processing
text:
5 Integrity checks

5.1 10. Duplicate rows in HH (hard stop)
dups <- duplicated(d2)
if (any(dups)) stop("Duplicated rows found in HH data - data file is corrupt")
Any duplicated row in the Haul Header table causes an immediate error. This is the strictest check in the pipeline.


5.2 11. Hauls without length records (warning)
After constructing haul.id, HH hauls that have no matching HL records are identified and printed as a warning:
diff <- setdiff(levels(d2$haul.id), levels(d3$haul.id))
if (length(diff) > 0) {
    cat("========= WARNING: ============\n")
    cat("Hauls without length info will be interpreted as empty hauls:\n")
    print(diff)
}
These hauls are retained in HH and treated as zero-catch hauls — consistent with the “zero-station” concept used in dr_cpue_length().


5.3 12. HL haul level consistency (hard stop)
stopifnot(nlevels(d3$haul.id) == nrow(d2))
After alignment, the number of distinct haul levels in HL must equal the number of rows in HH. Failure would indicate a mismatch between the exchange tables.


5.4 13. CSV file row-count integrity (readICES)
When reading from a flat CSV exchange file, the function counts header lines and data rows and checks they account for every line in the file:
if (sum(sapply(d, nrow)) + length(i) != length(lines))
    stop("csv file appears to be corrupt.")


5.5 14. Unique haul IDs when combining datasets (c.DATRASraw)
When merging two or more DATRASraw objects with c(), a pre-flight check ensures no haul.id appears in more than one object:
testUniqueHaulID <- function(args) {
    x <- lapply(args, function(x) levels(x$haul.id))
    if (length(unique(unlist(x))) != length(unlist(x)))
        stop("Haul ids must be unique.")
}


5.6 15. Missing haul IDs in CA (fixMissingHaulIds)
Older DATRAS CA submissions sometimes omit the full haul key. The package attempts to impute missing haul.id values by fuzzy-matching on (StatRec, Year, Quarter, Country, Ship).
Two modes controlled by strict:

strict = TRUE (default): only uniquely matched CA records get a haul ID; ambiguous matches are left as NA and warned about.
strict = FALSE: ambiguous matches receive a randomly chosen candidate haul; a fallback on Roundfish area is attempted for still-unmatched records.

A warning reports counts: total missing, uniquely matched, randomly assigned, and permanently unmatched.

title: D2.2 — Data Formats and Metadata
text:
1 Executive Summary
This document is IMBUS Deliverable D2.2 (Data Formats and Meta-data), addressing WP2 objectives 2 and 3 (see Background and Purpose). It documents the current ICES DATRAS exchange format and its metadata — providing a field-by-field reference for the HH (haul header), HL (haul-level catch at length), and CA (catch at age) record types.
The scope of D2.2 is the exchange data itself: the current field names, types, units, valid values, known issues, and the survey coverage available through DATRAS. The proposed IMBUS standardised data product (parquet files, derived CPUE pathways, intermediate data tiers) is specified in the companion deliverable D2.3 (D2.3 — IMBUS Integrated Data Product Specification, due August 2026).
The principal documentation findings are:

Two co-existing naming conventions. DATRAS field names changed around 2020 (e.g. Ship → Platform, HaulNo → HaulNumber). Both conventions are documented throughout, with legacy names shown in parentheses.
HL structure. The HL table combines haul join keys, species identification, sampling protocol bookkeeping, catch totals, and length frequencies in a single flat structure. These are documented as distinct field groups with known interpretation pitfalls.
Sentinel value −9. Used throughout DATRAS for missing or inapplicable fields; not a real value.
Species resolution via WoRMS AphiaID. Historical species codes (ITIS TSN, NODC) are mapped to current WoRMS AphiaIDs in the field aphia (Valid_Aphia).
DataType field. The DataType field in HH governs how several HL fields must be interpreted; it is the most common source of silent errors in user code.
Two interim canonical names (sex, aphia). Where the ICES “new” field names are inconsistent across tables or products, IMBUS adopts a single name as a temporary measure pending resolution by the ICES Datacenter — see IMBUS interim canonical names.

title: D2.2 — Data Formats and Metadata
text:
2 Background and Purpose
The ICES DATRAS database holds fisheries-independent bottom trawl survey data submitted by national institutes across the Northeast Atlantic, covering surveys from 1965 to the present. The data are structured as three exchange tables — HH, HL, and CA — which together describe each trawl haul, its catch by length class, and biological measurements on individual fish.
WP2 has four objectives:

Assess the user requirements of different user groups with respect to potential applications of survey data. (Addressed in D2.1, April 2026.)
Develop a data format that can be used to generate the products described in WP3–5.
Generate meta-data descriptions of the overall data.
Process the current data available in the DATRAS database into the new format, while correcting for any errors detected and taking account of zero observations and length/weight conversions.

Objective 1 has been delivered in D2.1 (IMBUS user requirements, April 2026, n = 55 respondents), which identified four dominant user challenges:

Complex table structure (HH/HL/CA hierarchy and join logic)
Column name changes introduced around 2020 (legacy names vs. “new” names)
Quality-control inconsistencies
Slow downloads

The current deliverable D2.2 addresses objectives 2 and 3 — the current data formats and the associated meta-data descriptions. D2.2 covers the three exchange tables (HH, HL, CA), their field-level metadata, and known issues with the current format. The proposed IMBUS standardised data product (parquet files, CPUE pathways, unique haul identifier) is covered in D2.3. A full scope statement is in Appendix 2.

3 ICES DATRAS Data Formats and Meta-data Descriptions
The ICES DATRAS database distributes bottom trawl survey data as three exchange tables. Each table is submitted independently per survey, year, quarter, and country; the tables are linked by a common set of haul identification fields. The following sections describe the current format of each table field by field, the metadata available for the surveys covered, and known issues with the current formats.
The field specifications below are drawn from two machine-readable metadata sources maintained in {obus}: dr_lookup_fields (field names, types, and descriptions — see Field and vocabulary reference) and dr_lookup_vocabulary (controlled vocabularies for categorical fields — see Field and vocabulary reference).

3.1.1 HH — Haul Header

3.2.2 Field and vocabulary reference
{obus} exposes the DATRAS field-level and vocabulary metadata as two data objects:
dr_lookup_fields is the complete field dictionary for all DATRAS exchange and derived product tables (HH, HL, CA, FL, LT, CPUEL, CPUEA, IDX). For each field it records the standard name (new), the legacy name (old), the data type (chr/int/dbl), and a plain-English description. The primary source is the ICES DATRAS web service endpoint getDatrasFieldList (https://datras.ices.dk/WebServices/DATRASWebService.asmx/getDatrasFieldList), which covers the formal upload schema for HH, HL, CA, and FA. This is supplemented by hand-curated entries for tables and fields not covered by the upload schema: LT and FL (returned by icesDatras helper functions), the derived products CPUEL, CPUEA, and IDX, and the Valid_Aphia / aphia mapping — a field added by the ICES datacenter during processing that is absent from the formal upload field list. The script that builds dr_lookup_fields is data-raw/DATASET_lookup_fields.R in the {obus} repository.
dr_lookup_vocabulary provides the controlled vocabularies for categorical DATRAS fields — i.e. the valid codes and their descriptions for fields such as HaulValidity, DataType, LengthCode, Gear, and Country. The source is the ICES Vocabulary service, accessed via the icesVocab R package (getCodeTypeList() + getCodeList()). The full ICES vocabulary is filtered to the subset of code types whose variable names correspond to fields in dr_lookup_fields, giving one row per valid code value. The building script is data-raw/DATASET_vocabulary.R in the {obus} repository.
library(obus)

# Field dictionary: names, types, descriptions for all DATRAS tables
dr_lookup_fields

# Controlled vocabularies: valid codes for categorical fields
dr_lookup_vocabulary
These two objects together constitute the machine-readable metadata layer underlying the field tables in Data Formats. Both are regenerated by sourcing the respective data-raw/ scripts against live ICES web services; the versions shipped with {obus} reflect the state of those services at the time of the last package build.
The build scripts apply corrections and additions to the raw web service output; see Appendix 2 — Build script deviations for the full account.

3.3.1 Column naming convention
Two naming conventions exist in DATRAS, reflecting a change introduced by ICES around 2020:

The co-existence of both conventions means that code written against one naming scheme fails silently or with cryptic errors against the other. All field tables in Data Formats list both names.

3.3.3 The DataType field
DataType is set at the haul level (HH) and governs how NumberAtLength, TotalNumber, and SpeciesCategoryWeight in HL must be interpreted. It is the single most common source of silent errors when working with exchange data, because the numeric meaning of HL fields depends on a field in a different table.

Size-stratified subsampling under DataType R. The DATRAS schema designates DataType P for hauls processed with size-stratified subsampling4, and most such hauls follow it: GB-SCT vessels (293 groups across NS-IBTS, SCOWCGFS, SCOROC — where a group is a unique combination of haul, species, sex, developmental stage, and species category) submit size-stratified hauls correctly as DataType P. In practice, however, a minority are submitted as DataType R — 95 groups (24.4% of the 389 size-stratified groups), predominantly DK vessels (82 groups, from 2024 onward), plus a handful from NL, BE, and NO. These are not data errors — the row-level formula NumberAtLength × SubsamplingFactor remains correct regardless of DataType. The risk arises only from direct use of TotalNumber, which reflects the stratum total, not the species-haul total, in these records.
The R code used to derive these statistics is in Appendix 2.
DataType must be joined from HH before any HL arithmetic:
hl |> left_join(hh |> select(.id, DataType, HaulDuration), by = ".id")

Across HL and CA:

Gear fields duplicated across HH, HL, and CA:
Gear, GearExceptions, SweepLength, and DoorType appear in all three tables with identical values. This is a submission artefact. HH is the sole source of truth; the HL and CA copies are redundant after joining on .id.


3.3.5 HL grouping key constancy violations
The sampling protocol fields are in principle constant within a natural group (.id × aphia × sex × DevelopmentStage × SpeciesCategory), but empirical checking reveals two important exceptions:

SpeciesValidity varies within 2,786 of the ~2.6 million total groups (0.1%), predominantly BTS (1,289 groups) and Can-Mar (1,272 groups). The most common co-occurrences are {1, 5} (1,281 groups) and {4, 7} (580 groups), reflecting the coexistence of full length-frequency rows and supplementary rows (totals-only, presence/absence) within the same group. This is by design in those surveys.
SubsamplingFactor varies within 389 of the ~2.1 million valid groups (0.02%) due to size-stratified subsampling — small and large fish are subsampled at different rates within the same species group (defined as .id × aphia × sex × DevelopmentStage × SpeciesCategory). This pattern occurs predominantly in GB-SCT vessels (293 groups, across NS-IBTS, SCOWCGFS, SCOROC) and DK vessels (82 groups, from 2024 onward in NS-IBTS and BITS). By DataType it splits as P (293 groups, 75.3% — all GB-SCT, the intended encoding), R (95 groups, 24.4% — predominantly DK; see The DataType field), and C (1 group, 0.3%); 293 + 95 + 1 = 389.
TotalNumber and SpeciesCategoryWeight also vary by stratum (104 of the ~2.1 million valid groups, 0.005%) as a direct consequence. The safe formula for the haul-level total is always n_haul = sum(NumberAtLength × SubsamplingFactor) applied at the individual row level — this is correct whether or not size-stratification is present.

The R code used to derive these statistics is in Appendix 2.


3.3.6 Other known data issues

SubsamplingFactor = NA: Approximately 0.015% of HL records have missing SubsamplingFactor under DataType R (Norwegian and Dutch vessels in NS-IBTS). This propagates as NA in computed n_haul and n_hour.
TotalNumber rounding for DataType C: TotalNumber is a back-converted CPUE count; arithmetic checks reveal rounding differences of 1–20 fish (~1% of DataType C groups). This is an artefact of the ICES submission process and is expected.
CA AreaCode/AreaType: CA rows can represent area-pooled age samples, not individual haul observations. Check AreaType before joining CA to HH.
Area standardisation: Mapping from haul positions to C-squares and ICES divisions is not provided in the current DATRAS exchange format; this is addressed in D2.3.

4 Task-level Assessment

4.1 T2.1 — User Requirements Survey
Proposal commitment: Survey data users across institutions to identify requirements and prioritise user needs; results to feed D2.2 format design and WP3–5 product scope.
Status: Complete.
D2.1 was delivered in April 2026 (Month 6, on schedule). 55 respondents were surveyed. Four dominant user challenges were identified:

Complex three-table structure (HH / HL / CA hierarchy).
Inconsistent column naming (legacy vs. post-2020 standard names).
Quality-control inconsistencies.
Slow data downloads.

These findings directly shaped D2.2’s scope (field documentation, naming harmonisation, sentinel value handling) and the D2.3 product design (parquet format, pre-computed CPUE tiers, composite haul key).



4.2 T2.2 — Data Format Design
Proposal commitment: Design a new data format capable of generating products for WP3–5, including handling zero observations and error corrections.
Status: Substantially complete — minor open items remain.
D2.2 documents the current DATRAS exchange format in detail (HH, HL, CA record types), and D2.3 specifies the IMBUS proposed format. The following design decisions are documented and implemented:

Unified column naming — standard names applied across all surveys and record types. Naming map maintained in {obus} as dr_lookup_fields.
Parquet distribution — columnar format enabling fast, column-selective queries without full downloads.
Sentinel value removal — DATRAS sentinel value −9 replaced with proper NA.
Species standardisation — historical numeric codes mapped to WoRMS AphiaIDs.
Unique haul identifier — 8-field composite key (Survey:Year:Quarter:Country:Platform:Gear:StationName:HaulNumber) resolves all known haul-join ambiguities.
DataType-aware CPUE — transparent CPUE calculation handling DataTypes C, R, S, and P correctly, including size-stratified subsampling.

Zero observations are handled via HH left_join HL in dr_cpue_length(): hauls with no catch for a target species appear as length_mm = 0, n_haul = 0, n_hour = 0 (zero-fill by design).
Open items:

CA section stub — completed 2026-06-20: CA now has the same subsection structure as HH and HL (haul ID, species ID, area/individual ID, length/sex, age determination, biological measurements, administrative).
Resolved (2026-06-19): aphia and sex confirmed as IMBUS canonical names for the WoRMS AphiaID and sex fields in both HL and CA (interim pending IMBUS project approval).
Action point A2: confirmation pending from Vaishav Soni and Adrianna Villamor on SubsampledNumber, SubsampleWeight, DevelopmentStage prevalence, and LengthType in CA.




4.3 T2.3 — Metadata Documentation
Proposal commitment: Generate metadata descriptions of overall data, including survey coverage, temporal range, and data quality characteristics.
Status: Substantially complete for HH and HL; CA pending.
D2.2 documents metadata at two levels:
Survey-level metadata — statistics for all 29 DATRAS surveys: year range, number of valid hauls, distinct AphiaIDs. NS-IBTS is the largest (36,566 hauls, 1965–present); CODS-Q4 the smallest (42 hauls, 2024). BTS is the most species-rich (1,012 AphiaIDs). A 30th entry, NS-IBTS_UNIFtest, is a test survey (5 hauls) and flagged for upstream filtering.
Field-level metadata — HH and HL exchange tables are documented field-by-field with: - Field name (legacy and proposed standard) - Data type, units, vocabulary where applicable - DataType dependencies (HL) - Known issues and data quality caveats (~20 specific issues identified with mitigations)

Per-survey fact sheets (coverage maps, gear history, time-series breaks, QC caveats) were identified as a user requirement (UR-Q1) but are deferred to further work; they are not explicitly scoped as a D2.2 deliverable in the proposal.
